name: VyOS
summary: Open-source network operating system (NOS) based on Debian GNU/Linux, combining FRRouting dynamic routing (BGP, OSPF), the NFTables firewall and multiple VPN protocols under a hierarchical transactional CLI interface.

content.introduction: VyOS is an open-source network operating system (NOS) designed to turn standard x86-64 or ARM computer hardware, as well as virtual machines and cloud instances, into professional-grade routers, firewalls and VPN gateways. Born in late 2013 from a community split following the abandonment of Vyatta Core after its commercial acquisition, VyOS has established itself as a software reference for interconnecting enterprise networks, data centres and telecommunications infrastructures.
content.what_is_it: Technically, VyOS is built on a customised Debian GNU/Linux base equipped with a hardened Linux kernel optimised for high-throughput network flow processing. Rather than forcing the administrator to handle the configuration files under `/etc/` individually, VyOS unifies all the network daemons under a declarative and transactional management framework. Its application core (`vyos-1x`), developed in Python 3 and C, ensures the dynamic compilation of the configuration parameters towards the components of the host system and orchestrates the persistence of the network state.
content.dynamic_routing_and_frrouting_stack: For advanced routing functions, VyOS integrates the FRRouting (FRR) software suite, the direct successor of Quagga and GNU Zebra. The platform exhaustively supports all the major dynamic routing protocols of the Internet, both in IPv4 and in IPv6: BGP (Border Gateway Protocol with granular prefix filtering by regular expressions, community attribute manipulation and RPKI validation), OSPF (OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 multi-area), IS-IS, RIP, RIPng and Babel. VyOS also supports policy-based routing (PBR), equal-cost multi-path load balancing (ECMP) and the VRRP high-availability and default gateway redundancy protocol.
content.firewall_filtering_and_nat: Perimeter security and packet filtering in VyOS rest on the Netfilter subsystem and the modern NFTables engine of the Linux kernel. The platform offers a firewall with stateful inspection capable of analysing flows by sequential rules or through a zone-based firewall architecture. Network address translation features cover source NAT (SNAT/Masquerade), destination NAT (DNAT/Port Forwarding), one-to-one NAT (1:1 NAT), as well as IPv6 transition mechanisms such as NAT64 and NPTv6. VyOS also integrates rate limiting, QoS packet marking and the synchronisation of conntrack connection tables between several nodes in high availability.
content.vpn_protocols_and_secure_tunneling: VyOS integrates an exceptionally wide range of secure interconnection and tunnelling protocols. For point-to-point and nomadic virtual private networks, it offers native support for WireGuard directly integrated into the Linux kernel for modern encryption at very high performance, as well as a complete IPsec stack powered by StrongSwan (supporting IKEv1, IKEv2, VTI virtual tunnel interfaces, BGP over IPsec and centralised RADIUS/EAP authentication). Added to these are the OpenVPN protocols (client and server modes), L2TP/IPsec, GRE, VXLAN for data centre network overlays, and IPv6/IPv4 encapsulation tunnels (SIT, IPIP, IP6IP6).
content.cli_experience_and_netdevops_automation: The management ergonomics of VyOS stand out through its modal hierarchical command-line interface (CLI) inspired by JunOS. It rigorously separates the operational mode for consultation and diagnosis (`show`, `monitor`, `ping`) from the configuration mode (`configure`, `set`, `delete`). The modifications made remain in an unvalidated buffer until the execution of the atomic `commit` command, with the possibility of instant cancellation (`rollback`) in case of error. For automated deployment (NetDevOps) and cloud virtualisation environments (KVM, VMware, AWS, Azure, GCP), VyOS offers a complete RESTful HTTP API, certified Ansible automation modules and Terraform providers making it possible to integrate routing into infrastructure as code (IaC) chains.
content.history_and_release_names: The project was born in 2013, when Brocade discontinued the community edition of Vyatta: a team of engineers took over the last community version and published VyOS 1.0 on 22 December 2013. The official page retraces the following milestones: Hydrogen in 2013, Helium in 2014, Crux in 2019, Equuleus in 2021, Sagitta in 2024 and Circinus in 2026. These names serve as major version markers in the project documentation.
content.release_channels_rolling_and_lts: Two channels coexist. The online documentation corresponds to the "rolling release" version, updated continuously. LTS versions are distributed separately: VyOS 1.5.1 LTS can be downloaded from the support portal and through the AWS, Azure and Google Cloud marketplaces. The project indicates that access to LTS versions is also open to contributors, within the framework of contribution counterparts.
content.distribution_and_deployment_targets: VyOS is deployed on standard x86-64 hardware, on virtual machines and in public clouds. The official page cites the AWS, Azure and Google Cloud marketplaces, as well as a deployment on the Dell NativeEdge offering for edge computing. The distribution model rests on system images updated by the mechanism specific to VyOS, independently of the Debian repositories of the underlying distribution.
content.documentation_structure: The user guide is organised into stable sections: history, first steps, installation and image management, quick start, command-line interface, overview and configuration guide, operational mode, automation, troubleshooting, configuration plans, VPP data plane, development and contribution. A section dedicated to coverage control and to writing documentation also appears in the guide.
content.image_based_package_delivery_and_update_: VyOS does not expose a distribution package manager to the administrator. The unit of deployment is the system image: `add system image` fetches an image from a URL or a local file, or accepts the keyword `latest`, and the configuration survives the operation. The `latest` keyword resolves through the URL set with `system update-check url`, which the documentation shows pointing at the rolling-release version metadata for AMD64, and the note attached to that option requires the URL to be configured for the installed release; after rebooting, the running image is read back with `show version`. The update-check URL therefore has to match the branch the system is meant to follow, and an installation kept on a numbered release is not served by the rolling metadata.
content.system_image_layout_and_boot_architectur: An installation keeps one directory per system image rather than overwriting a single root filesystem. The documentation describes the boot device holding a `/boot` directory with GRUB and a squashfs image named after the build, for example `2025.07.16-0020-rolling.squashfs`; each image directory contains the kernel, a compressed root filesystem and a directory for persistent storage such as the configuration. During boot the system extracts the OS image into memory and mounts the live-rw subdirectories that hold persistent configuration, which the documentation presents as the reason the system starts from a fixed, non-persistent image. Several releases can coexist on one device: `show system image` lists them with the default and running flags, `set system image default-boot` chooses the image started at the next boot, and `delete system image` removes an unused one.
advantages: Fully software solution freeing itself from closed proprietary network hardware and restrictive licence costs.
Exhaustive dynamic routing stack powered by FRRouting (BGP with RPKI, OSPFv2/v3, IS-IS, Babel, VRRP).
Hierarchical transactional command-line interface with atomic validation (`commit`) and cancellation (`rollback`).
Extended native support for multiple modern industrial VPN protocols (WireGuard, IPsec IKEv2, OpenVPN, VXLAN).
Adaptability to virtualised environments (KVM, Proxmox, VMware ESXi) and to public cloud instances.
Modular design fully automatable by means of a REST API, Ansible and Terraform for NetDevOps.
disadvantages: Absence of an integrated web graphical interface (GUI) by default, administration requiring command-line or API skills.
The business model reserves the stable precompiled long-term production images (LTS) for paid subscriptions (although the source code remains freely compilable).
Sustained learning curve for administrators not familiar with the modal hierarchical network configuration syntax.
Requires solid skills in network architecture and in Linux subsystems for in-depth diagnosis of packet flows.
Does not provide a ready-to-use deep packet inspection (DPI) engine or intrusion prevention system (IPS) in the system core.
who_is_it_for: Network engineers, infrastructure architects and system administrators managing enterprise networks or data centres.
Internet service providers, telecommunications operators and cloud hosting companies deploying virtual BGP transit routers.
NetDevOps teams looking for a software router programmable through REST API, Ansible and Terraform for their automation pipelines.
Advanced computing enthusiasts and homelab managers wishing for a robust and scriptable edge router for their local network.
who_is_it_not_for: Beginner or novice users looking for a simple firewall gateway fully configurable with the mouse through a web interface (pfSense or OPNsense being more accessible).
Small structures lacking network engineering skills and requiring immediate telephone assistance without a publisher contract.
Individual office workstations or computing machines not performing any gateway or network routing role.
Environments requiring ready-to-use application-level web content filtering features (stream antivirus, parental filtering).
content.verdict: VyOS is an open-source software router. By unifying on a hardened Debian base FRRouting, NFTables and WireGuard under a transactional command interface and an API, it addresses enterprise routing deployments.
